title: B1 Writing Quiz 1 — Work, Travel & Everyday Decisions

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I had more free time, I would learn to paint.
If I have more free time, I would learn to paint.
If I had more free time, I will learn to paint.
If I would have more free time, I would learn to paint.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I had more time, I would learn to paint.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I had studied harder, I would pass the exam.
If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
If I studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
If I would have studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If I had studied..., I would have passed.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This product is made in three different countries.
This product makes in three different countries.
This product is making in three different countries.
This product made in three different countries.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is made in three countries.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The report was written by our team last week.
The report wrote by our team last week.
The report was wrote by our team last week.
The report is written by our team last week.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was written by our team.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The manager who hired me has left the company.
The manager which hired me has left the company.
The manager whom hired me has left the company.
The manager, who hired me, has left the company but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The manager who hired me...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My colleague, who speaks four languages, is moving abroad.
My colleague who speaks four languages is moving abroad but.
My colleague, that speaks four languages, is moving abroad.
My colleague which speaks four languages, is moving abroad.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'who' for people: 'My colleague, who speaks four languages, is moving abroad.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She isn't answering, so she must be busy.
She isn't answering, so she must to be busy.
She isn't answering, so she must busy.
She isn't answering, so she must being busy.
questions.explanation: 'Must' + base verb expresses a confident deduction: 'she must be busy.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He might be stuck in traffic.
He might being stuck in traffic.
He might to be stuck in traffic.
He mights be stuck in traffic.
questions.explanation: 'Might' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'he might be stuck in traffic.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've written three emails this morning.
I've been writing three emails this morning.
I've wrote three emails this morning.
I'm writing three emails this morning already.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've written three emails.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've been working on this project for two weeks.
I've worked on this project since two weeks.
I'm working on this project for two weeks already.
I've been work on this project for two weeks.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been working... for two weeks.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have finished the project.")
options: He said that he has finished the project.
He said that he had finished the project.
He said that he finished the project already.
He said he have finished the project.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'he had finished the project.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "Where do you work?")
options: She asked me where do I work.
She asked me where I worked.
She asked me where did I work.
She asked me where I work.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'she asked me where I worked.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to work in retail before I became a teacher.
I use to work in retail before I became a teacher.
I was used to work in retail before I became a teacher.
I used to working in retail before I became a teacher.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to work in retail.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm still getting used to waking up early for work.
I'm still getting used to wake up early for work.
I'm still get used to waking up early for work.
I'm still used to get waking up early for work.
questions.explanation: 'Get used to' is followed by a gerund: 'getting used to waking up early.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We had to put off the meeting until next week.
We had to put the meeting off until next week away.
We had to put off to the meeting until next week.
We had to put the meeting until next week off.
questions.explanation: 'Put off' means 'postpone': 'put off the meeting until next week.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My sister looks after my children on Fridays.
My sister looks my children after on Fridays.
My sister looks after to my children on Fridays.
My sister after looks my children on Fridays.
questions.explanation: 'Look after' means 'take care of': 'looks after my children.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite the traffic, we arrived on time.
Despite of the traffic, we arrived on time.
Although the traffic, we arrived on time.
Despite the traffic was heavy, we arrived on time.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the traffic, we arrived on time.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The flight was delayed. As a result, we missed our connection.
The flight was delayed, as a result we missed our connection.
As a result the flight was delayed we missed our connection.
The flight was delayed as a result, we missed our connection.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'The flight was delayed. As a result, we missed our connection.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We don't have enough time to see everything.
We don't have time enough to see everything.
We don't have enough of time to see everything.
We haven't enough time to see everything.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough time.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The two job offers are similar in terms of salary.
The two job offers are similar in terms about salary.
The two job offers are similar in term of salary.
The two job offers are similar on terms of salary.
questions.explanation: 'In terms of' + noun means 'regarding': 'similar in terms of salary.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a new business contact you haven't met?
options: Hey there,
Dear Mr. Rahimov,
Yo,
Hiya,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Mr./Ms. [Surname],' is a respectful, semi-formal opening for a professional contact.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email to a business contact you know by name?
options: Yours faithfully,
Kind regards,
Later,
Talk soon,
questions.explanation: 'Kind regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering if you could send me the file.
I was wondering if you could to send me the file.
I was wondering could you sending me the file.
I wonder if you send me could the file.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could send me the file.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the client.' and 'The client's company won the award.'?
options: This is the client whose company won the award.
This is the client who company won the award.
This is the client which company won the award.
This is the client's company who won the award.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the client whose company won the award.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have never been to Japan before.
I have been never to Japan before.
Never I have been to Japan before.
I have been to Japan never before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never been to Japan.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the flight has been delayed.
I'd like to know whether has the flight been delayed?
I'd like to know, whether the flight has been delayed.
I'd like to know whether the flight has been delayed?
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time next week, I ___ on a beach in Turkey.
options: will lie
will be lying
am lying
lie
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be lying'.

questions.question: By the time we land, we ___ for over ten hours.
options: will travel
will have travelled
travel
are travelling
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have travelled'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly, we need a budget. Secondly, we need a timeline. Finally, we need approval.
Firstly we need budget secondly timeline finally approval.
Finally we need a budget, firstly a timeline, secondly approval.
Secondly firstly we need budget, finally approval timeline.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't mind helping me with this, would you?
You wouldn't mind helping me with this, do you?
You wouldn't mind helping me with this, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't mind helping me with this, will you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't mind..., would you?'
